answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine thought of Marcus Aurelius, from Meditations, Book VII, 67. The tidy modern phrasing is a lightly modernized rendering of the Greek; the public-domain George Long translation (1862) reads “very little indeed is necessary for living a happy life.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: c. 170–180 AD, during Marcus’ military campaigns

source.excerpt: Nature has not so mingled the intelligence with the composition of the body, as not to have allowed thee the power of circumscribing thyself and of bringing under subjection to thyself all that is thy own… Always bear this in mind; and another thing too, that very little indeed is necessary for living a happy life.
trail: The passage is authentic: Meditations Book VII, 67, where George Long’s 1862 translation renders it “very little indeed is necessary for living a happy life.”
Wikiquote lists it in its sourced section, keyed to Book VII, 67, with the Greek original ἐν ὅλιγίστοις κεῖται…

The clean popular wording — and the tail “it is all within yourself, in your way of thinking” often appended to it (as on Goodreads) — is an interpretive paraphrase, not a verbatim line from a standard translation.
source.excerptNote: Meditations VII.67, George Long’s 1862 translation. The familiar “Very little is needed to make a happy life” is a smoother modern rendering of the same sentence.

source.rightsNote: Meditations was composed in Greek around 170–180 AD and the original is long in the public domain. The oldest widely quoted English translations — including George Long’s of 1862, which carries this passage as “very little indeed is necessary for living a happy life” — are also public domain in the United States. The tidy modern wording is a light paraphrase of that public-domain text.

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.heading: About the author
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 AD and the last of the “Five Good Emperors.” His Meditations — private notes written in Greek to himself, largely on campaign — became the most widely read work of Stoic philosophy. Book VII gathers reflections on self-sufficiency and the inner sources of contentment, the vein this line belongs to.

misattribution.heading: Wording & the appended tail
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Marcus Aurelius is correct — this is genuinely from Meditations VII.67. What drifts is the exact wording.

items.why: “Very little is needed to make a happy life” is a smoothed rendering; the public-domain George Long translation reads “very little indeed is necessary for living a happy life,” and other translations render the same Greek differently again.

The tail “it is all within yourself, in your way of thinking” is frequently tacked on (e.g. on Goodreads) but does not appear verbatim in the standard published translations of VII.67; it is an interpretive addition.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea and the passage are authentically Marcus Aurelius (Wikiquote, sourced section, Book VII, 67); only the exact English wording is a later tidy-up.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Coming from the most powerful man in the Roman world, the claim that happiness needs “very little” carries extra weight. In Book VII, 67 Marcus argues that a good life is not blocked by lack of leisure or learning: what is truly one’s own — one’s judgments — is always within reach.

The surrounding sentence stresses self-sufficiency: nature lets you “circumscribe” yourself and govern what is your own, so even an emperor’s contentment rests on inner disposition, not on external abundance.
